DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection

The study is clearly structured and most of the cost arithmetic checks out. However, several of its central claims are contradicted by its own data. The tonnage projection, the treatment arrangement and the "fully funded" conclusion all need reworking before Cabinet is asked to approve anything.

## Critical issues

**1. Participation in flats was not "broadly similar". It was a third of the rate in houses.**
Table 1 shows 66% participation in houses and 21% in flats. Flats that did take part also produced less (1.4 kg vs 1.9 kg). Section 2 says "participation was broadly similar across housing types", and Section 7 concludes the service "can be delivered on a uniform basis." The data supports the opposite conclusion. Flats need a different approach, such as communal bins, different container sizes, or engagement with managing agents. Roughly 10,400 households (20% of 52,000) are affected. The author's summary repeats this claim, so it is a misreading of the results, not a typo.

**2. The projection uses a 64% participation rate that the pilot never produced.**
Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was 57% (2,280 / 4,000). The 3,290-tonne figure only works at 64%:

- 52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks ≈ **3,290 t**
- 52,000 × 57% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks ≈ **2,930 t**
- By housing type (41,600 houses at 66% × 1.9 kg; 10,400 flats at 21% × 1.4 kg) ≈ **2,870 t**

The pilot's flat share (20%) matches the district's, so 57% is the directly applicable figure. Using the housing-type split is more defensible still. The "All" row's 1.9 kg is also rounded up: the weighted average is about 1.86 kg. Tonnage is overstated by roughly 13–15%. That contradicts the claim that projections reflect "how Thornbury residents actually behave."

**3. Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage.**
Section 4 states that Brookfield can offer only **1,800 t/year** until 2029. Projected tonnage is 2,870–3,290 t, which leaves 1,070–1,490 t a year with nowhere identified to go. The study does not address:

- where the surplus goes (the next AD plant is 46 miles away),
- the gate fee there,
- the extra haulage, vehicle time and crew time for a 92-mile round trip, which could need extra vehicles or bulking/transfer.

So "treatment is local" is only true for about 55–63% of the tonnage. The £243,000 saving assumes every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38.

**4. The disposal saving is overstated, so the net cost is understated.**
The saving is £74/t × tonnage.

| Scenario | Saving | Net cost |
|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t) | £243,000 | £490,400 |
| 57% participation (~2,930 t) | ~£217,000 | ~£517,000 |
| Housing-type split (~2,870 t) | ~£212,000 | ~£521,000 |

The higher net costs are before any cost for the surplus tonnage. Even before treatment and haulage costs for that surplus, the corrected net cost reaches or exceeds the £520,000 provisional allocation. The £30,000 headroom in the study disappears once the tonnage error is fixed.

**5. "Fully funded" rests on a provisional allocation.**
The Government "has indicated" funding, and the £520,000 is "provisional." Section 7 and the author's summary present this as settled. Cabinet should be told:

- whether the allocation is confirmed,
- how long it lasts (new-burdens funding is often time-limited or tapered),
- whether it covers capital or only revenue,
- what happens if it comes in lower.

There is no sensitivity analysis and no contingency.

## Significant issues

**6. Table 2 is not "every cost line".** Missing or unexplained items include:

- spare vehicle or cover for breakdowns, servicing, sickness and leave (six vehicles and six crews leaves no resilience),
- supervision, management and admin,
- the dedicated phone line and web page (Section 6),
- recruitment and training costs,
- haulage and gate fees for tonnage beyond Brookfield's capacity,
- vehicle financing costs (only straight-line depreciation is shown),
- one-off costs of delivering caddies to 52,000 households, unless these are inside the £88,000 "annualised" line, which should be broken out,
- clarity on whether £34,000 per operative includes employer on-costs.

**7. The timetable has no slack.** Vehicles ordered by December 2026 arrive in March 2027. Crews are trained "on the new vehicles during March", and collections start the week of 5 April. Any slip in delivery delays the launch. Caddies also go to all 52,000 households in the same month. The study, dated October 2026, should state:

- the supplier's confirmed lead time,
- a contingency plan (hire vehicles, phased start),
- whether the December order deadline is achievable given Cabinet scheduling.

**8. Statutory deadline compliance is not addressed.** Section 1 cites the legal requirement but does not say what the deadline is, or whether an April 2027 start complies. Under the Simpler Recycling reforms, most English councils were expected to start by 31 March 2026 unless a transitional arrangement applied. If Thornbury is relying on an extension or transitional arrangement, the study should say so.

## Minor issues and evidence quality

- **Seasonality and novelty.** The pilot ran January–June only, with no summer or autumn data. Participation often falls after the launch period. Weekly figures are averaged, so the trend over the six months, which matters most, is not shown.
- **Satisfaction survey.** "81% of surveyed pilot households" gives no sample size, response rate, or split by participants and non-participants. Responses are likely skewed towards participants.
- **Contamination.** "Under 2% in spot checks" should give the number and timing of checks, and whether results differed for flats.
- **Pilot ward selection.** The wards were three "deliberately mixed" wards, but the study gives no evidence that they are representative of the district on other factors, such as deprivation or rural/urban split.
- **Possible upsides not counted**, such as reduced residual collection frequency or tonnage effects. These could help the case and are worth noting.

## Recommendation to the author

Before this goes to Cabinet:

1. Rewrite the participation finding and propose a separate approach for flats.
2. Recalculate tonnage from the actual pilot rates, ideally by housing type, with a sensitivity range.
3. Resolve treatment for tonnage above 1,800 t, and cost the haulage and gate fees.
4. Complete the cost table, including resilience, management and contact centre costs.
5. Present the funding position as provisional, with a downside scenario.
6. Add timetable contingencies and confirm the statutory deadline position.

With the corrected figures, the service appears to need more funding than the provisional allocation provides. That should be stated plainly in the recommendation.
